summary: The PCE architecture is set out in RFC 4655 and extended in RFC 5623 and RFC 6805, but they leave some questions unanswered, especially about how the architectural views interact. This document discusses those open questions.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7399 collects the questions that the path computation element architecture never answered. It asks where a path computation element gets its picture of the network, how a router finds one, what happens when there are several, how the hierarchy of domains is organised, and what changes when the element keeps state. For each question it sets out the options and what the existing work suggests.

what questions does the pce architecture leave open
subtitle: The questions the path computation element architecture left open, and how the pieces might be combined.

tldr.problem: The path computation element architecture and its two extensions deliberately leave some questions unanswered, especially about how the components find each other, what they share, and who owns them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7399 lists those questions one at a time and discusses each in the light of the existing architecture, other components, existing protocols and recent IETF work.
tldr.outcome: The document updates nothing and defines no new protocol elements. It offers a map of the open questions, a comparison of the stateless and stateful modes of a path computation element, and a set of suggestions about how the components could be combined for more advanced function.

today: RFC 7399 is an Informational RFC published in October 2014, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It is a discussion document: the questions it lists were open when it was written, and it does not claim to close any of them.

sections.title: Why the Questions Are Written Down
sections.content:
The path computation element architecture was documented in RFC 4655. It was extended for multi-layer networking with the Virtual Network Topology Manager in RFC 5623, and generalised to hierarchical operation in RFC 6805. Many people have joined the working group since then and want to use or understand the architecture, and they have missed the discussions that shaped it, so they are unfamiliar with the questions that were raised along the way.

These three views of the architecture deliberately leave some key questions unanswered, particularly about how the components interact. This document draws those questions out and discusses them against other architectural components, existing protocols and recent IETF work. It does not update the architecture documents and it does not define how protocols or components must be used. It does suggest how the components might be combined to provide more advanced function.

The readers are assumed to know the terminology of RFC 4655, RFC 4726, RFC 5440, RFC 5623 and RFC 6805, with more on stateful operation in the stateful PCE work. One term is used in a particular way: the word area covers both an OSPF area and an IS-IS level.
sections.plainLanguage: The architecture for delegating path computation to a separate server was written down years ago, and later work extended it to several network layers and to hierarchies of networks. Those documents left gaps. This one lists the gaps so that newcomers to the working group do not have to rediscover them, and offers what the existing work suggests as answers.

sections.title: What the Topology Database Holds
sections.content:
A path computation element computes paths from a view of the available network resources and topology, and that view is collected into a Traffic Engineering Database, or TED. RFC 4655 does not say in detail what goes into it, only that it holds the topology and resource information of the domain. The precise contents depend on the kind of network and on the computation that has to be performed. At a minimum the database holds the nodes and links that make up the domain and identifies the connectivity within it.

For most traffic engineering needs, such as MPLS traffic engineering, the database would also hold a basic metric for each link and the resources still available on it. More advanced cases may need qualitative information: link delay, link jitter, the throughput a node can handle, optical impairments, switching capabilities, or limited cross-connect capability between nodes.

One element matters especially for protected services, the Shared Risk Group, which marks resources that share a risk of failure from a single event. In short, the database needs whatever the requested computation and its objective functions demand. That is not always trivial: in some optical networks, computing a path for a new label switched path may have to consider the effect that turning up a new laser has on the optical signals already carried by the fibres. That information can be abstracted as parameters of the links and nodes, or it may be easier to hold it in a database of the paths already in place.
sections.plainLanguage: The server needs a picture of the network before it can choose a path. At the very least that picture has the nodes and the links between them. For traffic engineering it also needs a cost for each link and how much capacity is left on it. Richer computations need more, such as how much the path would cost in delay or how likely two links are to fail together.

sections.title: How the Topology Database Is Filled
sections.content:
One way to build the database is for the element to take part in the interior gateway protocol of the network. In an MPLS traffic engineering network that means OSPF TE or IS-IS TE, and in a Generalized MPLS network the Generalized MPLS extensions to those protocols. Taking part, even as a passive receiver, places a significant load on the element, because the protocol is chatty when the network changes often and the element must parse messages and update the database. It also means the implementation must support two interior gateway protocols.

The alternative offered by BGP-LS is to let a BGP speaker that already takes part in the interior gateway protocol, such as a border router or a route reflector, filter and aggregate the topology according to policy and advertise it northbound to the element. The element then needs only a simplified subset of BGP rather than two full interior gateway protocols. BGP may not be convenient everywhere, for instance in an optical network or a core that runs no BGP, and not all relevant information is carried by the standard traffic engineering extensions. In those cases the database has to be built or supplemented from other sources, such as the network management system, inventory systems, or data configured directly. It has also been proposed that the PCE Communication Protocol itself be extended to collect information from network devices, since they may already speak it and could report the resources and state they see.

The topology may also include links that are not real cables. A virtual network topology is a set of hierarchical paths created in one network layer to give flexibility to another. A traffic engineering link may therefore be a real data link, a path in a lower layer, or a path that could be set up on demand when it is needed, which is called a virtual traffic engineering link. The element may prefer real data links, because they are more stable, or dynamic lower-layer paths, because those can be repaired dynamically, and it may want extra indicators in the database to help it choose.
sections.plainLanguage: The picture of the network can be built in three ways. The element can listen to the routing protocol the network already runs, which is accurate but heavy and means implementing two protocols. A router that already speaks the routing protocol can filter the information and send it northbound over BGP, which is lighter. Or the information comes from management systems and configuration. Some of the links in the picture are not real cables but paths that would be created in a lower layer on demand.

sections.title: Finding, Choosing and Grouping Path Computation Elements
sections.content:
A path computation client must know where its element is, because the communication protocol is transaction based, carried over TCP, and the architecture requires targeted exchanges. The client can be configured with the address of its element, which is light but prone to configuration errors and does not satisfy minimal-configuration operation, and configuring several elements and coping with their failures is worse. The architecture also allows elements to advertise themselves in the interior gateway protocol, which works where that protocol is in use and the element takes part in it. Where it does not, some other announcement or discovery function is needed, and a directory system such as DNS is suggested, as used for the discovery of location servers and in the ALTO discovery function.

When more than one element is known, the client has to choose. Any algorithm will do, such as first listed or round robin, but elements may differ in capability and in the scope of what they can compute, so the client wants the one most likely to satisfy the request, starting with the requirement that it can compute paths for the domain at all. Elements can announce their capabilities as flags in their advertisement, but flags carry only the core capabilities, so more detailed capabilities, such as the ability to compute point-to-multipoint paths, are announced as optional type-length-value objects in the opening message of the communication protocol. The exchange is an announcement and not a negotiation: a client cannot ask an element to support something it has not announced. A client may also vary which element it uses according to reported load, but the document warns that in an overloaded system this simply moves the overload, so some discretion is needed. Sending every request to every known element and taking the first answer would overload them all, and sharing the load is one of the reasons to have several.

Several elements in one network raise the question of whether their databases agree. The database reflects the state of the network and is not a booking system, so the system as a whole does not prevent two computations from competing for the same resource during provisioning. The elements could share one database, which is unlikely to be efficient, build their own, which is likely to give small and temporary differences because they attach to the routing protocol at different points, or synchronise explicitly from a master, which is a mirrored database with all the problems that brings. Given that the provisioning protocols already handle contention, that differences are likely to be small, and that contention is unlikely except in busy networks, the document suggests there may be no value in synchronising the databases at all.

The document then turns to questions of hierarchy and destination. A path computation element responsible for several domains needs information from each of them. In a multi-domain network, a path has to be found to the domain that holds the destination, and the per-domain method requires only that each element knows the next domain on the way; how it determines that is not obvious. The backward recursive method gives better paths but needs to know in advance which domain holds the destination and the sequence of domains leading to it, and none of the ways of establishing the domain sequence addresses the question of where the destination lies. The document notes that a call, as defined for label switched paths, is carried as an ordinary IP message and its response can carry the identity of the domain holding the destination, which may be a way of finding out. In a hierarchy, a parent element coordinates with child elements and keeps a map of the child domains; who runs it depends on whether the domains belong to one provider or to several, and the architecture does not require a parent to see inside a child domain. The child must be configured with the address of its parent and must be authorised to peer with it, and the parent must know the identities and credentials of its children, or hold a shared secret. The parent map is likely to rely on administrative configuration and commercial agreements, though a routing protocol inside the parent domain and exports from the child domains can also feed it. Applying the hierarchical model to the Internet is not considered feasible; a rough guide is around 20 domains at most, and it is hard to construct practical examples with more than two or possibly three levels.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that wants a path computed must find the element that will do it, and if there are several it must pick one that has the capability it needs. The capabilities are announced rather than negotiated, so the router chooses from what is on offer. When several elements run in one network their pictures of the network will differ slightly, and the document concludes that making them identical is probably not worth the trouble. The same questions come back when the network is split into domains: who runs the element that ties the domains together, how do they find each other, and how does anyone know which domain the destination is in.

sections.title: State, Delegation and Policy
sections.content:
A stateless element can take other paths into account if they are supplied with the request, which helps when arranging protection paths that share no links, and when reoptimizing a group of paths at once, but reporting many paths is a heavy burden on the protocol messages. A stateful element keeps a database of the paths that are active in the network, so a client can refer to one by its identifier alone. That database also lets the element balance the distribution of paths and place new ones where there is room.

Building that database is a problem in itself. The simple answer is for every ingress router to report the paths it sets up, modifies or tears down, using the state report message defined for the purpose. It gets harder where routers do not support the protocol, do not support the report, or were told to set up a path with a pre-computed path by a management system. Any router on a path can probably see the whole path through the record route object and knows the bandwidth reserved, so any of them could report it, and a path reported more than once does no harm because it is clearly identified. Even so, some paths may cross only routers that know nothing about the element, and then the element has to read the MPLS and GMPLS management information modules instead. The document concludes that there may be no substitute for every router being aware of stateful elements and able to answer requests for reports, which lets the database be built from nothing at the start of day and checked against the network after an outage.

Two elements keeping state has to be synchronised, and since both may be creating entries, the synchronisation has to be incremental and bidirectional rather than a dump. A passive element only answers requests; an active one issues recommendations to the network, which may be a new path for an existing path or a path for a new one. Many people hold that an element cannot be active, because its job is only to compute paths, and that the active part is a separate component; the Virtual Network Topology Manager is such a component in some configurations. LSP delegation is the process where a client hands responsibility for updating a path to the element, which must then be both stateful and active; the element sends a new path with the instruction to re-signal, and the client is expected to act on it, though the document notes the question of who owns the path is not settled. The comparison table in the document draws the six combinations of passive or active with stateless or stateful, and concludes that the modes in which the element itself instantiates paths are out of scope: it can recommend, but not create.

Scheduling paths ahead of time raises the same problem of holding resources. Pre-signalling so that each router holds a reservation needs multi-dimensional state on every node, while a central database with time-based booking works if the element is also active. Policy enters everywhere: which computations a client delegates, which elements it uses, which clients an element serves, what it collects and trusts, which objective functions it applies, what state it keeps, and which paths it may change. The document's summary is that a path computation element is substantially a policy engine that computes paths.
sections.plainLanguage: An element that keeps no state has to be told about every other path in the network before it can avoid clashing with them, and that is a lot of reporting. An element that keeps state learns the paths from the routers themselves and can then place new ones more carefully. Making that work means every router in the path has to report what it sets up. An element can also be active, meaning it recommends paths to the network rather than only answering questions, and when a client has delegated a path to it, the element expects the client to act on its advice.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The effect of a path computation element on network security has to be considered in the context of the existing routing and signalling protocols. Multi-domain scenarios and the relationships between clients and elements may increase the network's exposure to attack. This document defines no new protocol elements or mechanisms, so it introduces no new security issues, and security is treated as a question already answered by the earlier work, even if the answers are not perfect. The earlier documents considered security in the architecture itself, in discovery, and in the communication protocol.

One point stands out: the communication protocol runs over TCP. An analysis of the security issues of routing protocols that use TCP, including this one, exists, as does an experimental approach to giving it a secure transport.

Several of the questions the document raises need to be read with security in mind. The topology and other information about the network must be kept private and protected from modification or forgery, which means access to the topology database and the path database must be secured, and the mechanisms used to gather information must include security. Discovery must be protected against impersonation or misconfiguration, so that clients know they are getting correct paths and elements know they are serving legitimate requests. The synchronisation of information and state between elements is subject to the same requirements, because what is exchanged is sensitive. Where the element computes paths for components that provision the network, those components are responsible for the security of the provisioning mechanisms. And where the element interfaces with other components, those external communications need to be secure too.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no new mechanisms, so it adds no new security problems, but it flags where existing ones land. The picture of the network is sensitive and must not be altered or forged, so the databases and the way they are filled have to be protected. Discovery has to be safe against someone pretending to be the element, and the traffic between elements has to be protected as it crosses the network.
